package_info.why_malicious: MikuBot is a Windows-based malware bot designed to steal sensitive data, enable remote access, propagate via USB, and download or execute additional malware. It employs anti-detection techniques such as encrypted strings, dynamic API resolution, and anti-emulation, and is distributed as a commercial crimeware product.

execution_context.file_location: RCData section of the Windows PE resource section

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code accesses the RCData resource section, retrieves an encrypted payload, decrypts it, and loads the UPX-packed payload into memory for execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Legitimate software rarely stores encrypted executable payloads in resource sections and decrypts them at runtime.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not self-decrypt and execute hidden payloads from resource sections.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some DRM-protected or anti-tamper software may use similar techniques for code protection.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code creates a uniquely named mutex to ensure only one instance of the malware runs and to protect the code from being modified.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Malware commonly uses mutexes to prevent multiple infections and to coordinate persistence.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications may use mutexes, but not with random or unique names tied to malware persistence.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate software may use mutexes for single-instance enforcement.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
// Pseudocode: Create scheduled task for persistence
schtasks /Create /SC MINUTE /MO 10 /TN "MikuBotMutexName" /TR "C:\Path\To\MikuBot.exe"
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code creates a scheduled task named after the mutex to execute the malware every 10 minutes, ensuring persistence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Creating scheduled tasks for self-execution is a common malware persistence technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software rarely schedules itself to run every 10 minutes without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System maintenance tools may use scheduled tasks, but with clear user intent.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code collects sensitive information from the victim and sends it to a remote command and control server via HTTP.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exfiltrating sensitive data to an external server is a hallmark of information-stealing malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not send user data to unknown remote servers without consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Crash reporting or telemetry (with user consent) may send limited data.
key_indicators: Outbound HTTP requests to untrusted domains

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
// Pseudocode: Launch hidden VNC session
StartHiddenVNCSession(); // Accepts remote connections for control
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code launches a hidden VNC session, allowing remote actors to access and control the victim's machine.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Hidden remote access is a core capability of RATs and is highly suspicious.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate remote access tools require user consent and visibility.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: IT support tools, but with user awareness and consent.

execution_context.file_location: main process memory, USB device mount points

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code enumerates connected USB drives, copies itself to them, and sets up autorun for propagation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Self-propagation via USB is a classic worm technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not copy itself to removable drives or set autorun entries.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Portable applications (with user intent), but not silent propagation.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code downloads additional malware from the Internet and executes it on the victim's machine.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Downloading and executing arbitrary code is a primary method for malware to escalate or diversify attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not download and execute code from untrusted sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Software updaters (with signed payloads and user consent).

attack_chain.action: Malware is executed, decrypts and loads its payload from the resource section.
attack_chain.leads_to: Payload is unpacked and executed in memory.

attack_chain.action: Creates a mutex to ensure only one instance runs and to protect code integrity.
attack_chain.leads_to: Prevents multiple infections and coordinates persistence.

attack_chain.action: Establishes persistence by creating a scheduled task to run every 10 minutes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ensures malware re-executes even after reboot.

attack_chain.action: Collects sensitive data from the victim and exfiltrates it to the C2 server.
Launches a hidden VNC session for remote access and control.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker can interact with the victim's system in real time.

attack_chain.action: Propagates itself to USB drives for further spread.
attack_chain.leads_to: Infection spreads to new hosts via removable media.

attack_chain.action: Downloads and executes additional malware as instructed by the attacker.
attack_chain.leads_to: System may be further compromised with new payloads.

behavioral_signatures: Executable decrypts and loads payload from resource section at runtime
Creation of uniquely named mutexes to prevent multiple instances
Scheduled task creation for frequent self-execution (every 10 minutes)
Hidden VNC server launched without user notification
Enumeration and writing to USB drives with autorun setup
Outbound HTTP/S requests to unknown or suspicious domains
Download and execution of additional binaries from the Internet
file_indicators: Presence of encrypted data in RCData section of PE files
Scheduled tasks with unusual or random names
Unexpected autorun.inf files on removable media
network_indicators: HTTP/S POST requests to attacker-controlled C2 domains
Unusual VNC traffic from non-standard ports
Frequent outbound connections after process startup
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for executables that decrypt and execute payloads from their resource sections, create mutexes with random or suspicious names, and establish scheduled tasks for persistence. Watch for hidden VNC server activity, USB propagation behaviors, and outbound connections to untrusted domains. File system monitoring for self-copies and autorun files on removable media, as well as network monitoring for C2 communications and VNC traffic, can help identify infections.
